- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.3) or volatile, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer below forecast or anticipate sharper drops.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >70), model frequently overcorrects with a steep upward trend; cap forecast growth after peak or introduce lagged decay.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 30d drop from 76+ to 70+), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecast to reflect recent volatility decay.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows rapid divergence, sentiment may be misleading; use sentiment as signal to adjust horizon-specific bias (e.g., 10d vs 30d).
- For 30d forecasts, if model starts at 72+ and true outcome drops below 70, consider sentiment decay as a trigger to reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- If sentiment history shows repeated peaks followed by sharp drops, model often fails to anticipate reversal; add early warning signal for mean reversion in 10-15d horizon.
